# What Am I Giving Up?

> "However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ."
>
> — Philippians 3:7

NOTHING. Not one thing.

That's the whole chapter, really. But you don't believe it yet, so let's go slowly.

Stopping looks hard for one reason: fear. You're afraid a pleasure is about to be taken off you, or a comfort you lean on. You're afraid that the quiet evening alone, the long shower and the warm bed will never feel quite as good again. You're afraid that the next rotten day will arrive and you'll have nothing to take the edge off it.

Underneath those sits a bigger fear, and it's the world's favourite lie: that an orgasm on demand is something a man can't do without. That if you stop, you'll be denying your own nature, and you'll walk around with a hole in your life where the habit used to be.

Get this straight in your head:

**THE HABIT DOESN'T FILL A HOLE. IT DIGS ONE.**

Think about the body you've been given. All the laboratories on earth together can't assemble one living cell, never mind an eye or a child. If you believe God made you, then he made your desire as well, and he made it to carry you out of yourself and towards a wife. If you're an atheist, play along: call it nature, and notice that nature didn't design the system to be run solo, nightly, off a memory.

C.S. Lewis has a senior devil admit as much to a junior one, speaking of God: "He made the pleasures: all our research so far has not enabled us to produce one." Hell can't make a pleasure. All it can do is take a real one and bend it. And the bent version, the same devil says, has a signature: "it diminishes pleasure while increasing desire."

You know that signature. Every year you get less out of the habit and want it more.

## There's nothing to give up {-}

Once the Little Monster has starved and the Big Monster has been cleared out of your head, you won't want to jerk off. You won't be resisting it. You simply won't want it, the way you don't want to chew your pen.

Look at where the habit leaves a man. On the nights he does it, he's miserable afterwards: flat, guilty and a bit disgusted. On the nights he tries not to, he's miserable too, because he feels robbed. He has only two kinds of evening and both are bad. One man described the first kind in a single line:

> "This empty dumb feeling when it's over… & there's nothing left."
>
> — a man on a NoFap forum

You've seen the smoker at a wedding who keeps finding reasons to step outside. Nobody watching thinks, "Lucky fellow, off to enjoy himself." They think, "Poor man, he can't sit through the speeches." Now think of yourself at a family gathering, slipping off upstairs with your phone. You weren't doing that for the fun of it. You did it because you were uncomfortable without it. No free man behaves like that.

**"But I'd be giving up sex."** No. If you're married, you're about to get it back. The habit has been quietly spending, alone, what belongs to the two of you. Lewis drew a sharp line between wanting a woman and wanting a sensation. The man after the sensation, he said, "wants a pleasure for which a woman happens to be the necessary piece of apparatus." Jerking off cuts out even the apparatus. Ask the men who've stopped what happened to the real thing. One wrote that he'd gained a "stronger real sex drive without wanting an easy release like porn". A married man put it more plainly: "sex feels natural and great with wifey".

**"But I'm single. It's all I've got."** Then what you've got is a rehearsal for being alone. A Catholic speaker named Jason Evert says it kindly: "What you really long for is authentic love, but you settled for the counterfeit." The counterfeit trains you to be content without the real thing.

**"But I'd be giving up part of being a man."** It's the other way round. A man led about by an itch is less of a man, and he knows it. You aren't handing in your manhood. You're collecting it.

So there's nothing to give up. And there's a great deal to gain. When men think about stopping, they tend to think first about energy or sleep, or about their conscience. Those are good reasons. But I believe the biggest gains are these:

- Your confidence and your courage come back.
- You stop being a slave.
- The dark thing lurking behind every thought, and the daily contempt for yourself that goes with it, are gone.

## Void, the beautiful void! {-}

Imagine you get an itchy patch on the back of your hand. It's nothing much. A friend hands you a little tube of cream and says, "Try this." You rub some in and the itch stops at once. Marvellous.

A few days later the itch is back, and a bit bigger. You use the cream again. Gone again. Your friend tells you to hang on to the tube.

And so it goes. Each time the patch comes back, it has spread a little further and it itches a little harder, and the gap between flare-ups keeps shrinking. After a few years it covers both arms and wakes you most nights. The cream still works, for a while. So you keep a tube in every coat. You won't travel without one. You get nervous when a tube is nearly empty. Nothing touches the itch but the cream.

Then one day you read something. It turns out thousands of people have this same rash, and the cause has finally been found. The cream doesn't cure the itch. It pushes it under the skin for a few hours, and feeds it while it's down there. The cream is the reason the rash has been spreading. Stop using the cream and the rash dies off by itself, quite quickly.

Would you use the cream again?

Would you need willpower to leave the tube in the drawer? Would you count the days? You might be a little uneasy for the first week, in case what you'd read was wrong. But as soon as you saw the patch shrinking, the uneasiness would go, and the wish for the cream would go with it. Would you mope? You'd be delighted. You'd had something you thought you were stuck with for life, and it's clearing up. Even if it took months to fade, you'd look at your arms every morning and grin.

That is exactly what it's like to stop jerking off.

The rash isn't the guilt, the tired mornings, the wasted evenings, the distance from your wife or the silence between you and God. All of those are extra. The rash is that edgy, hollow, slightly panicky feeling of *I need it*. Men who don't have the habit never get that feeling. You didn't have it at nine years old. It arrived with the first time, and every time since has fed it.

The feeling you keep reaching to relieve is the void. Here is the beautiful part: the cream made it. When you stop, the void doesn't yawn open in front of you. It closes.

A few men will tell you they're perfectly happy as they are. Look closer. They're the man with a tube in every coat, explaining that he just likes the smell.

Now read the verse at the head of this chapter again. Paul had a list of things he'd once counted as profit. He didn't give them up with gritted teeth. He looked at them beside what he'd found, moved the lot to the other side of the ledger, and in the next verse called them "refuse", which is a polite translation. He isn't boasting about a sacrifice. He has seen what the stuff was worth.

That's where you're headed. You won't be a man bravely doing without. You'll look at the tube of cream and wonder how you ever thought it was medicine.

It is a fine thing to be free!
